Rectify

/REK-tuh-fy/ — rhymes with fly, stress on first syllable · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To rectify something is to correct a mistake or fix a problem so that it is right again.

The bank rectified the billing error within a day.

Worked Example

When the lab discovered that their measurements were incorrect, they immediately rectified their calculations and resubmitted the accurate results.

Rectify captures both the correction of the mistake and the restoration of things to a right or correct state. Fix is too vague; correct alone doesn't emphasize the sense of making things right again.

Antonyms

How Strong Is It? — break → distort → rectify → perfect

break vs. rectify

break vs. rectify: Break sits at the opposite end of the scale from rectify: breaking creates the damage, while rectifying sets the resulting wrong right again.

distort vs. rectify

distort vs. rectify: Distort also points the opposite way from rectify — distorting twists something out of its true shape, while rectifying straightens the mistake back out.

perfect vs. rectify

perfect vs. rectify: Perfect goes further than rectify: to rectify an error is to make it right, but to perfect something is to polish it until it is flawless.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — rect

Root — rect: straight, right (Latin)

Suffix — -ify

Suffix — -ify: to make (from facere) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Rectify joins the Latin root rectus ('straight, right') with -ify ('to make'): to rectify a mistake is literally to make it straight and right again.

Use the root in a new word: rectangle

Use the root in a new word: rectangle: A rectangle is a shape made of straight sides and right angles — the same root rectus, 'straight, right,' that you set back in place when you rectify a mistake.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal

Rectify is for correcting errors and restoring things to a right state—it's more formal and precise than plain fix. Use it when you're emphasizing that a mistake was made and must be corrected, especially in professional or formal contexts. For casual situations, fix or correct works fine.
